methods.label: Use integer powers and check the base
methods.explanation:
Assume first that \(\log\) means the common logarithm \(\log_{10}\). We will prove the inequality using integer powers.

For a positive integer \(n\), the binomial theorem gives a useful bound. For \(1\le j\le n\),
\[
\binom nj n^{-j}
\le \frac{1}{1\cdot2\cdots j}
\le 2^{1-j}.
\]
The first inequality follows because each numerator factor in the binomial coefficient is at most \(n\). The second follows because every denominator factor after the first is at least \(2\). Summing these bounds gives the finite geometric sum
\[
\left(1+\frac1n\right)^n
\le 1+\sum_{j=1}^{n}2^{1-j}
=3-2^{1-n}<3<\sqrt{10}.
\]

Now let \(0<u\le1\), and let \(n=\lfloor1/u\rfloor\), the greatest integer at most \(1/u\). Then \(n\ge1\) and
\[
\frac{1}{n+1}<u\le\frac1n,
\qquad \frac1{2n}\le\frac1{n+1}<u.
\]
Since common logarithms are increasing, the integer-power bound implies
\[
n\log_{10}(1+u)<\frac12.
\]
Thus \(\log_{10}(1+u)<\frac1{2n}<u\).

For any \(x>0\), choose a positive integer \(m\ge x\) and put \(u=x/m\). Then \(0<u\le1\). The binomial expansion has nonnegative terms, so
\[
1+x=1+mu\le(1+u)^m.
\]
Taking common logarithms now gives
\[
\log_{10}(1+x)
\le m\log_{10}(1+u)<mu=x.
\]
Therefore D holds for every positive \(x\) under this convention. At \(x=9\), the values \(\log_{10}10=1\), \(9/10\), and \(9\) rule out A, B, and C.

The unspecified base matters. If the base is \(2\), then \(x=1\) gives \(\log_2 2=1\), ruling out A, B, and D as universal statements. Also, \(x=3\) gives \(\log_2 4=2<3\), ruling out C. Thus base \(2\) gives E. The conditional answer is D for common logarithms, but the displayed statement needs a base convention for a unique answer.
